# Can LLM judges recover capability from saturated benchmark outputs?

## Summary

Yes. 

* Judges rank most pairs correctly once their question votes are pooled. 

But

* Much of what judges respond to is writing style with no detected capability signal.   
* Adding more question samples helps with reducing noise to a point but doesn’t help with residual error.   
* Adding more judges doesn’t help with residual error either.  
* Counterbalancing position bias helps more than a larger ensemble of judges.

## 1\. LLM judges recover capability information from correct answers

Rows are aggregated into one vote per question item, so the question is the sampling unit. The median question carries 16 rows across judges, presentation orders and length conditions.

![][image1]

Pooling every question vote ranks **21 of 25 pairs correctly**. If the answer text carried no capability information beyond correctness, this would sit near chance. So there is *something* that the judge is picking up on.

## 2\. More questions improve ranking, but systematic error remains

### How the pooling works, on one worked pair

Three judges, both presentation orders, so each question has six verdicts. A question with five of six verdicts for the stronger model has mean 0.83, above 0.5, so its vote is 1. Four of six also votes 1: the margin is discarded. Two of six votes 0, and exactly three of six keeps half a vote. One hard-majority vote per question.

Suppose the pair's pot of votes is 1, 1, 0 and 0.5, mean 0.625. The curve draws k votes, takes their majority, and repeats. At k of 1 the accuracy is the pot mean. As k grows the drawn mean converges to 0.625, so accuracy converges to 1. A pot mean of 0.47 converges to 0 the same way. The plateau height of a band is the share of its pairs whose observed question evidence points the right way.

The levels of the ensembling comparison differ only in which verdicts form the vote. A judge that always picks whichever answer is shown first looks perfect in one order and perfectly wrong in the other, and becomes an uninformative 0.5 once both orders enter its vote: counterbalancing acts inside a single judge. Other judges can then outvote what remains of its noise, but a question where every judge leans the wrong way stays below 0.5 at every level.

![][image2]

Accuracy rises as questions are pooled and then **flattens by about 30 distinct questions** under both capability labels. The draws are without replacement, so the axis counts distinct benchmark questions, and each curve ends at the pair's full observed verdict rather than a bootstrap extrapolation.

Under GPQA, sufficiently distant pairs become perfectly ranked. This does not survive when distance is defined by the Artificial Analysis index. Under both labels, pooling converges to each pair's own direction, and aggregation cannot correct a pair whose question-level evidence points the wrong way. Section 5 shows that for three of the four misranked pairs, disjoint question sets independently point the wrong way, so more questions from this distribution would not repair them.

## 3\. Counterbalancing position bias helps more than adding judges

Six of the 10 judges had notable position bias.

![][image3]

The pooled term alone reads as no position bias. The per-judge terms show most judges have one, and that they cancel because they point in opposite directions.

## 4\. Judge decisions depend on broad stylistic cues

The original four-predictor model shows the judge follows real capability, and also follows length after capability is accounted for.

![][image4]

The expanded analysis refits the judge model across 136 transcript features, each marginally and within its feature family. In the primary within-pair marginal analysis, 98 of 136 features were associated with judge choices. Of these, 71 had no detected association with held-out accuracy. We call these judge-choice features without a detected capability signal. Non-significance is not evidence that the true association is zero, so this is consistent with judge bias rather than a demonstration of it.

![][image5]

The judge responds to most of the writing-style features we measured, and no capability signal is detected for the large majority of them. The 136 features are correlated, so 98 associations do not represent 98 independent properties of writing. 

Each feature was also fitted jointly with its family and with the capability gap added:

![][image6]

Holding the capability gap fixed barely moves the typical coefficient. The judge's response to these features is therefore not a restatement of its response to capability. 

### Automatically discovered features tell the same story

The hand-built features are one description of a transcript. The capability analysis also has 240 TF-IDF topic components and 32 sparse-autoencoder latents learned from Qwen3-Embedding-8B embeddings of the same transcripts, both discovered from text alone. Refitting the judge model on every feature of each method, with the same fits and the same multiplicity control, gives the same decomposition:

![][image15]

The judge follows 140 of the 240 TF-IDF components, and 122 of those carry no detected capability signal. The SAE latents carry the most capability per feature, 14 of 32 track held-out accuracy, and the judge does proportionally better there: of the 17 latents it follows, 5 agree with capability, 3 point the opposite way and 9 have no detected signal. In every feature language, most of what the judge responds to is not capability.

## 5\. The main result survives alternative explanations

### An external capability label gives the same orderings

![][image7]

All 17 models were scored against the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1.1. The two measures place the same model ahead for **22 of 24** pairs with a defined direction. Pair ranking scored against the index is 18 of 24, against 20 of 24 for the GPQA label. The judge sides with GPQA on both disagreements. 

### Capability-label uncertainty isn’t enough to explain why it fails

The GPQA label is estimated from 198 items per model, so a close pair's ordering may not be established. Two estimates address this. An independent Beta posterior per model gives a posterior probability for each ordering. A paired bootstrap resamples the 198 shared questions and recomputes both accuracies together, which respects the pairing through question difficulty. The two disagree by up to 0.36, so the pairing matters, and the paired bootstrap is the primary estimate.

![][image8]

**20 of 25 pair orderings have paired-bootstrap support above 0.95**, and the judge ranks 17 of those correctly. One of the four ranking failures sits on a genuinely uncertain ordering, at 0.616. The other three have paired-bootstrap ordering probabilities of 0.997, 0.998 and 0.999. The judge reverses pairs whose ordering is established with very high support.

### The misrankings are not finite-question noise

A pair can also be misranked by chance in the judge votes themselves: a pair whose true vote rate is just above 0.5 can present observed questions just below it. Two checks separate that from systematic inversion, both resampling the unique questions.

![][image14]

Three of the four misranked pairs are systematically inverted. Their 95% intervals sit entirely below 0.5, and in 97 to 100% of random splits of their questions into disjoint halves, both halves independently point the wrong way. New questions from this distribution would not repair them. The fourth, gemini-2.5-flash against qwen3.5-122b-a10b, rests on only 20 questions; its interval crosses 0.5 and its halves never agree on the wrong direction, so that one is compatible with finite-question uncertainty. All 21 correctly ranked pairs keep their whole interval above 0.5.

### Row-level leakage does not explain the predictive performance

Leave-one-out holds out a single comparison row, and one question appears many times across judges, orders and length conditions. Grouped cross-validation tests whether that inflates the estimate. Each specification is reproduced with its own target, row set and position term, because the fits do not share them.

| Specification | random rows | hold out questions | hold out model pairs |
| :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: |
| headline, four predictors, target `chosen_left`, 97,698 rows | 0.6657 | 0.6656 | 0.6513 |
| marginal, log word count, target `is_correct`, 91,481 rows | 0.6402 | 0.6400 | 0.6264 |

Holding out whole questions changes accuracy by less than 0.0002. Holding out whole model pairs costs about 1.4 points, within the fold spread in both cases. The relationships transfer to unseen questions and held-out model pairs. A model may still appear in other pairs during training, so this does not establish transfer to unseen models.

The hierarchical fit reaches 0.677 while the corresponding fixed-effect logistic model reaches 0.640. The difference reflects additional hierarchical structure, including pooled per-judge effects and item random effects. We therefore do not interpret the 0.677 value as a grouped out-of-sample accuracy. Separately, grouped cross-validation of the fixed-effect specification shows that its predictive relationship is stable when entire questions or model pairs are held out.

## Additional detail

![][image9]

The distribution of leave-one-out accuracy across the 136 one-feature models. 

![][image10]

Features without a detected capability signal did not spread evenly across families. Answer-behaviour features, which describe what the answer does, are handled well. Features describing how the answer is written are where the judge goes wrong.

![][image11]

At 511 questions, showing each pair in both presentation orders is worth about 6 points over a single order. The judges share substantial systematic error, and an ensemble cannot cancel this.

![][image12]

Under the GPQA capability label, judge identity barely matters on pairs with bigger gaps but is very sensitive on close ones. Two judges are reliably inverted on close pairs. gpt-4.1-nano ranks 0 of them correctly and qwen-2.5-72b-instruct ranks 0.08. Both are near perfect on distant pairs. 

![][image13]

The GPQA-only pooling curve, for reference The wide-gap gradient it shows is specific to the GPQA label.
